paras: Where does our food come from? Today we follow food from the field to our plate, sing a funny poem about a BIG laddoo, and read about food made during festivals. Along the way we will also do a little maths and science.
Picture story: wheat grows in a field, the wheat is cut and made into flour, the flour is made into dough, and the dough is cooked into chapatti.

sections.heading: A. Look at the pictures and answer.

items.q: What can you see in Picture 1?
items.a: Teacher note: Children describe what they see in the picture (for example, a wheat field). Accept any answer that matches the picture.

items.q: Look at Picture 2. What is the man doing with the wheat?
items.a: Teacher note: Guide children to answer in a full sentence, for example, 'The man is cutting the wheat.' Check against the picture.

items.q: Look at Picture 4. Who are they? What are they doing?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers depend on the picture. Encourage a full sentence starting with 'They are ...'.

items.q: What is the girl doing in the last picture?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers depend on the picture. Encourage a sentence starting with 'The girl is ...'.

items.q: What do you have along with chapatti?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, dal, vegetables, curd, pickle). Let children share what they eat at home.

items.q: Have you seen a field? What was growing there? Speak about it.
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended speaking activity. Answers will vary. Encourage children to use describing words such as green, tall and big.

sections.heading: Science Corner: Where does the energy come from?

items.q: Plants need sunlight and water to grow. Which part of the day gives plants the most sunlight: morning, noon or night?
items.a: Teacher note: Noon is when the Sun is highest and brightest. Discuss how plants use sunlight to make food and grow.

items.q: Wheat becomes flour, and flour becomes chapatti. Name the steps in order using the words first, then, next and finally.
items.a: Teacher note: Sample: First, wheat grows in the field. Then, it is cut. Next, it is ground into flour. Finally, the flour is made into chapatti.

items.q: A family has 4 members. Each member eats 3 chapattis. How many chapattis are needed in all?
items.a: 4 x 3 = 12 chapattis.

items.q: If 2 chapattis are left over, how many chapattis were made altogether?
items.a: Teacher note: Children add 12 + 2 = 14 chapattis. Accept correct working shown in any form.

paras:
If all the laddoos were one Laddoo
Oh! What a BIG Laddoo it would be!

If all the children were one child
Oh! What a BIG child that would be!

If all the seas were one sea
Oh! What a BIG sea it would be!

Then if the BIG child
picked the BIG Laddoo

And threw it into the BIG sea
Oh! What a BIG SPLISH-SPLASH it would be!

sections.heading: B. Talk about it. Answer the following questions.

items.q: Have you seen a big laddoo? How big was it? Did you eat it all by yourself? Tell your friends about it.
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended speaking activity. Answers will vary. Encourage the use of big, bigger and biggest.

items.q: Have you eaten anything that is very big? What was it? Talk about it.
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended speaking activity. Answers will vary.

items.q: What different kinds of laddoos have you eaten?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, besan laddoo, motichoor laddoo, rava laddoo, coconut laddoo).

sections.heading: C. Name a few things that are round in shape. Can you eat all of them? Write them in the correct column.
sections.note: Teacher note: Add a two-column table image here with the headings 'That can be eaten' and 'That cannot be eaten'.

items.q: That can be eaten
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, laddoo, orange, tomato, idli, gulab jamun).

items.q: That cannot be eaten
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, ball, wheel, clock, coin, stone).

items.q: The child threw the Big Laddoo into the sea. What do you think happened to the Laddoo?
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended. Accept any sensible answer, for example, 'It sank', 'It melted', or 'It made a big splash'.

sections.heading: Science Corner: Splish-splash!
sections.note: Teacher note: Do this activity with a tub of water, a small ball (or small stone) and a bigger ball (or bigger stone). Children drop each object gently into the water from the same height and watch the splash and the ripples.

items.q: What happens to the water when an object falls into it?
items.a: Teacher note: The water splashes and makes ripples (small waves) that spread outwards. Children should describe what they actually see.

items.q: Which object made a bigger splash, the small one or the big one?
items.a: Teacher note: Usually the bigger and heavier object makes the bigger splash. Children should record what they actually observe.

items.q: What kind of splash would a BIG laddoo make in a BIG sea? Use the word splish-splash in a sentence.
items.a: Teacher note: Accept any correct sentence, for example, 'The big laddoo fell into the sea with a splish-splash.'

items.q: There are 12 laddoos. 4 children share them equally. How many laddoos does each child get?
items.a: 12 divided by 4 = 3 laddoos each.

items.q: One laddoo is cut into 2 equal parts. What do we call each part?
items.a: A half.

items.q: A laddoo is round like a ball. Which shape is a laddoo: a square, a triangle or a sphere?
items.a: A sphere.

items.q: Arrange in order from smallest to biggest: a laddoo, a cricket ball, a football.
items.a: Teacher note: Smallest to biggest: a laddoo, a cricket ball, a football (sizes may vary slightly). Ask children to use the words small, big and bigger.

paras: Sri Hari and Maha Lakshmi are friends. Maha Lakshmi cannot see properly. It was her birthday. Sri Hari gifted her a box of mixed sweets. She felt the sweets and excitedly picked up the big laddoo. She said, "I love laddoos!"
Sri Hari was surprised and asked her, "How did you know it was a laddoo?"
Laddoos are sweets, commonly eaten in every house.

sections.heading: E. Think and say what Maha Lakshmi answered.

items.q: How did Maha Lakshmi know it was a laddoo?
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended. Accept sensible answers, for example, 'I felt its round shape', 'It was big and soft', or 'I smelled the sweet smell'.

sections.heading: F. Write words that tell us about the laddoo.

items.q: The laddoo is ______.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, round, sweet, soft, big, yellow, tasty).

items.q: The laddoo is ______.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Ask children to write a different describing word.

items.q: The laddoo is ______.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Ask children to write a different describing word.

items.q: Maha Lakshmi used her sense of touch to know the laddoo. Name the five senses and the body part for each.
items.a: Sight (eyes), hearing (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue), touch (skin).

items.q: Which senses can you use to find out about a laddoo? Write one thing you learn from each sense.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Sample: touch tells us it is round and soft; smell tells us it is sweet; taste tells us it is sugary; sight tells us it is yellow.

items.q: Is a laddoo hard or soft? Is it rough or smooth? Is it light or heavy?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary with the type of laddoo. Let children feel a real laddoo if possible.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: The box of sweets

items.q: The box has 5 laddoos, 4 barfis and 3 jalebis. How many sweets are there in all?
items.a: 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 sweets.

items.q: Maha Lakshmi ate 2 sweets. How many sweets are left?
items.a: 12 - 2 = 10 sweets.

paras: Did you know that not only sweets but a few other dishes are also prepared especially during festivals?
Have you heard of khichdi? It is a popular dish. Khichdi is usually cooked with rice and lentils together. It is prepared during festivals and also eaten as a meal.
Festivals keep us connected with nature and culture. Every year we celebrate many festivals in our country. Festivals help us stay together. They bring happiness, joy and smiles.
Khichdi is a traditional dish prepared especially during the Sankranti festival. Different parts of India prepare khichdi with different variations, like adding vegetables or using different lentils.

Did you know that this festival is also known as the Harvest Festival? It is celebrated to thank the Sun God for a good harvest. It is known by different names like Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri, Bihu, Maghi Sankrant, Makara Sankranti, Sakraat and Magha Saaji across the country. Flying kites during this festival is also very popular.
Khichdi is known by different names across the country.

Gujarati khichdi, Gujarat.
Pongal, Tamil Nadu.
Bihari khichdi, Bihar.
Bajra khichdi, Rajasthan.
Kichuri, West Bengal.
Bisi bele bhat, Karnataka.
Moong khetchir, Kashmir.

sections.heading: I. Which is your favourite festival? Write the names of some sweets and dishes prepared on that day.

items.q: My favourite festival is ______________________.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Accept any festival.
Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, laddoo, payasam, puran poli, sevai, khichdi).

items.q: We use heat to cook khichdi. What happens to rice when it is cooked in water?
items.a: Teacher note: Rice absorbs water, becomes soft and gets bigger (swells). Children can compare dry rice with cooked rice.

items.q: What pushes a kite up into the sky?
items.a: The wind (moving air).

items.q: Can a kite fly high when there is no wind? Why or why not?
items.a: Teacher note: Usually not, because there is no moving air to lift it. Children can explain in their own words.

items.q: Sankranti is celebrated to thank the Sun God for a good harvest. Why is the Sun important for crops?
items.a: Teacher note: Plants need sunlight (along with water) to grow. Accept answers in simple words.

items.q: How many different names of khichdi are given in the list?
items.a: 7 names.

items.q: To cook khichdi, 1 cup of rice needs 2 cups of water. How many cups of water are needed for 3 cups of rice?
items.a: 3 x 2 = 6 cups of water.

items.q: Khichdi is made with 2 things together. Name them. If you add 1 vegetable, how many things are in the khichdi now?
items.a: Rice and lentils; with 1 vegetable added there are 3 things (2 + 1 = 3).
